text: You get a list of triplets, each one a, b, c, and a target triplet. In one move, you pick two different triplets, i and j, and you replace triplet j with the max of each position. You can do this as many times as you want. Return true if the target can show up in the list.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a move only uses max, position by position. So a number in a triplet can go up or stay the same, but it can never go down. Is that right?

Okay, that's the key thing for me. If a triplet has even one number bigger than the target at that spot, it's poison. The moment I merge it into anything, that spot is too big, and it can never come back down. So I should never touch it. And the target doesn't need to be one of the originals — it just has to appear after some merges. A triplet that already equals the target counts too, with zero moves. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten to the fifth triplets. Every value is between one and one thousand.

Got it. Values start at one, never zero — I'll keep that in mind. Quick check on the example: the triplets are two-five-three, one-eight-four, and one-seven-five, and the target is two-seven-five. The middle one has an eight where the target only allows a seven, so it's poison. Merging the other two gives exactly two-seven-five. So the answer is true, which matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to actually do the moves — keep merging pairs and collect every triplet I can reach. With a hundred thousand triplets, even one round of all pairs is about ten to the tenth merges. Way too slow. This problem reminds me of a greedy filter. Because max only goes up, there are just two kinds of triplets: poison ones I must skip, and safe ones, where every number is at most the target. A safe triplet can only push me closer, never past. So the greedy is: merge all the safe triplets. That's the biggest triplet I can build that stays under the target. If even that isn't the target, nothing smaller will be.

Here's the plan, in three steps. One: start a running answer at zero, zero, zero. Two: for each triplet, if all three numbers are at most the target, take the position-wise max into the answer; otherwise skip it forever. Three: return whether the answer equals the target. One thing worth flagging — the start value is a correctness detail. Start at one, one, one, and a lone poison triplet with target one-one-one gets skipped, yet the answer already looks like the target, so I'd wrongly return true. Zero is never a real value, so it can't fake a match. The trade-off: three found flags work too; both are one pass, and I'll keep max because it mirrors the move. Does this approach sound good?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop. The answer starts as three zeros. For each triplet, one if-statement checks all three positions against the target, joined with and; if it passes, I take the max into each slot. At the end I return whether the answer equals the target — vector equality compares element by element, so that last line is the whole check. The one detail worth flagging: I take each triplet by reference, not by copy. Each triplet is a vector, so copying it is wasted work. On a hundred thousand triplets, that's about zero point two milliseconds versus one point seven — around seven times slower for no reason.

Let's dry-run example one, target two-seven-five, expected true. The deciding step is the second triplet, one-eight-four: an eight where the target allows a seven, so I skip it and the answer stays two-five-three. Merging it would lock that spot at eight forever. The last triplet brings in the seven and the five, and I land on the target. True, as expected. Corner cases: every triplet poison — answer stays zeros, false. All safe, each position from a different triplet — true. A lone poison triplet with target one-one-one — false, exactly what a one-one-one start gets wrong. Safe triplets that never reach the last position — false.
How sure are you about the greedy?

Pretty sure, and here's the short proof. Any triplet I can build is a max of some originals. If one of them is poison, the result is poison too, so the target can only come from safe ones. And the max of all safe ones is at least as big as any group of them, while still at most the target. So if any group hits the target, the full group does too. I also checked it against a brute force that really does all the merges: on seven hundred fifty-one thousand, eight hundred fifty-three small cases, zero mismatches. The one-one-one start had twenty-one thousand, two hundred twenty — every one a false true on target one-one-one.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: each triplet gets three compares and up to three max calls. Space is constant extra — the answer is always size three. In the worst case all hundred thousand triplets are safe, and it's still one pass, around zero point two milliseconds. The biggest value is one thousand, so a plain int is plenty. Oh, one more thing — the order of the triplets doesn't matter. Max doesn't care about order, and the safe test looks at one triplet at a time, so this even works on a stream. I never need to sort or go back.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw right away that max only goes up, so any triplet above the target is poison forever, and you turned that into: merge every safe one, then compare. You flagged that starting the answer at zero is a correctness detail, with a concrete counterexample to prove it. And you showed the found-flags version is the same idea, and explained why. Good work.
